title: Cop31 told it risks being ‘ghost’ summit as all mentions of ‘fossil fuels’ removed from draft text
text:
Every mention of “fossil fuels” has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night, threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”.
The second draft of the key text, released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis.
Panama made the unusual move of writing to the Turkish and Australian presidents of the talks announcing that unless all its demands were met, it would block any outcome.
“We have listened carefully to the speeches of these days,” read the letter signed by Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro. “They are beautiful speeches. But while we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed … Outside this room and this conference, the world needs and expects radical change from us, and we are not delivering it.”
Cop negotiations require consensus, meaning that Panama’s stance, especially if supported by others, has the potential to upend the talks in their final hours.
The “cover decision” text is likely to be the main outcome of Cop31, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris agreement in limiting temperature rises and staving off the worst ravages of global heating.
But in slimming down by half an unwieldy 18-page first draft issued on Monday, the joint presidencies of Australia and Turkey cut many of the commitments – including a phaseout of fossil fuels, and stronger support for developing countries to adapt to extreme weather – that vulnerable countries were relying on.
Countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels at Cop28 in 2023, but negotiations since have failed to flesh out the ambition.
“Frontline communities will look on with despair,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank. “If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost Cop. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here.”
His verdict – that the talks had been “muzzled” by the refusal of some fossil fuel producing countries to allow a commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” to stand – was echoed by campaigners around the world.
Rachitaa Gupta, global coordinator of the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice, said: “The cause of the climate crisis is clear, as well as who should pay for it. What’s remaining is the global north’s political resolve to provide this finance. The moral bankruptcy of the global north is very visible to all of us in the global south.”
Campaigners urged developing countries to reject the new drafts and keep fighting for a better outcome. “We are on the brink of an outrageous and utterly embarrassing lack of leadership by the Cop31 presidencies,” said Andreas Sieber, of the campaign group 350.org. “They have reduced one of the defining challenges of our time to an inconvenient paragraph they would rather delete.
“Rich countries’ failure on finance [for poorer nations] is a historic disgrace. They expect developing countries to shoulder the cost of a global transition while refusing to provide the means to deliver it. This is not a failure of technical negotiations. It is a shameless abdication of political responsibility.”
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of the negotiations, laid the blame for the weak text firmly at the door of the countries present. “We have put forward what we think, based on all our consultations, gives us the best chance of the most ambitious results that consensus will allow,” he said.
His Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum, the president of the conference, said there was “great enthusiasm” among the countries negotiating, and that the latest text showed a “strong commitment to the Paris agreement”.
He defended the exclusion of the words “fossil fuels” by saying it had been agreed at previous Cops. “I don’t think there’s any backsliding,” he said.
The commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” was exchanged in the text for the much weaker pledge to an “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience”, though there was reaffirmation that the goal of holding global temperature rises to 1.5C above preindustrial levels would remain central – even though it is now certain to be breached.
The pledge that 35% of global final energy demand should be met by electricity from 2035 was downgraded to a voluntary option among a suite of measures.
In a packed afternoon on the penultimate official day of the fortnight-long talks, a separate negotiating strand on climate finance produced a largely empty document, showing nations had failed to make progress on delivering the $300bn a year developed countries have pledged to the developing world by 2035.
Separately, at a historic leaders’ summit in Shenzhen between China, the US and Russia, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin vowed to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. Tlou Ramaru of the African Group of Negotiators described this as “hypocrisy”.
As countries digested the contents of the draft texts, the dual Cop presidencies of Australia and Turkey began to hold meetings with the main negotiating groups and individual countries, which were scheduled to go on through the night on Thursday, and probably into Friday morning. Although the talks are scheduled to end on Friday at 6pm in Turkey, Cops have a habit of over-running.
